title: India's Next Rs.1,000-Crore Food Brand May Rise From the Freezer
excerpt: Protein-rich frozen foods, fuelled by quick commerce's insatiable freezer demand and a global shift toward high-protein eating, are emerging as the most lucrative corner of India's food industry.
body:
• India's next big food fortune is likely to be built on protein-rich frozen and ready-to-cook products, not on another flavour of chips.
  • The sector did roughly Rs.95,500 crore of business last year, growing more than 75 per cent year on year, according to Reuters reporting citing Datum Intelligence data.
  • A global shift toward high-protein, less-indulgent eating — accelerated by GLP-1 weight-loss drugs — is reaching India through gym culture and reformulated snacks rather than prescriptions.
  • The least glamorous players may win biggest: whoever solves cold-chain logistics for delicate frozen formats ends up owning the infrastructure every brand must rent.

The Freezer Economy

India's next food boom may not arrive on a snack shelf. It may arrive in a freezer. Every new dark store that a quick commerce platform opens comes with a freezer that has to be filled, and the sector did roughly Rs.95,500 crore of business in India last year, growing more than 75 per cent year on year, according to Reuters reporting that cites Datum Intelligence data. Less noticed than the delivery-speed wars is what the freezer requirement is doing to Indian food manufacturing: frozen parathas, marinated kebabs and ready-to-cook curries — niche indulgences a decade ago — are now shelf-fillers for an industry built on ten-minute delivery.

Context and Background: The Protein Pivot

What goes into those freezers is shifting in a specific direction. In the six months after starting GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, consumers globally cut spending on chips and savoury snacks by 11.5 per cent and sweet bakery products by 8.5 per cent, according to a McKinsey analysis published this year. Spending on yoghurt, fresh produce and meat snacks rose over the same period. The drugs are barely prescribed in India. But the appetite shift they represent — toward smaller portions, higher protein and less indulgence — is arriving anyway: through gym culture, reformulated snack launches from large Indian food companies, and what increasingly fills a quick commerce order.

Government policy has been nudging the sector in the same direction for years. The Production Linked Incentive scheme for food processing, backed by an outlay of Rs.10,900 crore, has helped create roughly 3.3 lakh direct and indirect jobs and pushed exports of approved processed food products to a compound annual growth rate of over 13 per cent since 2019-20, according to figures from the Ministry of Food Processing Industries. The categories the scheme prioritises — ready-to-cook and ready-to-eat foods, processed fruits and vegetables, and value-added protein products — are exactly the ones now benefiting from a consumer mindset shift policymakers could not have predicted.

"The next Rs. 1,000-crore Indian food brand won't be born from a flavour launch. It will be born from a freezer contract nobody bothered to write a press release about."

— NDTV Food

Impact and Analysis: Cold Chain as the Real Moat

The businesses that capture this opportunity are unlikely to be the ones with the flashiest branding. They will be the ones that solved the boring problem first: reliable cold storage, consistent blast freezing, and a supply chain that does not break down between a factory in a tier-two town and a dark store in a metro. India's cold chain was built for bulk commodities like potatoes and dairy, not the delicate, high-margin, ready-to-cook formats quick commerce demands. Whoever fixes that quietly ends up owning the infrastructure every food brand eventually has to rent.

There is also an export angle that gets underplayed. Global demand for convenient, protein-dense, shelf-stable Indian food is rising steadily, and a frozen category built on nutrition credentials travels beyond Indian borders in a way traditional namkeens and confectionery rarely managed.

Diaspora Angle

For the diaspora, the shift is visible in the freezer aisle of any Indian grocery store abroad. Frozen parathas, marinated kebabs and ready-to-cook curries are among the fastest-growing categories in NRI shopping baskets — a ready-made export market for an Indian frozen-food sector built on nutrition credentials.

What's Next

Watch where capital goes next. Quick commerce platforms keep opening dark stores, each one a new freezer to fill, and the PLI pipeline keeps expanding capacity for exactly the categories in demand. The brands that matter will be locking in cold-chain capacity and protein supply chains now — before the freezer aisle becomes the most fought-over shelf in Indian retail.
